The directing and artist duo fleuryfontaine use this surveillance footage and combine it with images retroactively animated using the Blender graphics software to take an almost forensic look at the positions that each of us takes in today’s artificial and security-fixated environment and that determine our behaviour, our body and our relationship with the world and other people. With its elegant and austere structure, the film insistently questions the excesses of the use of violence and its legitimacy in the police and other public organs.

The sun is shining and all the kids are playing happily all day long. At night they fall into their beds exhausted, carelessly kicking off their slippers. The next morning brings a surprise: All the slippers are gone! Well, it must have been Slipper Keeper Kitty who got them, the parents shrug. The children set out to find their shoes again …

When all pieces of the puzzle – surfaces, lights, shapes – have found the place that is uniquely their own, the magic begins: A multiverse opens up, insights flow and inventions are made. The magic touches inner and outer worlds, planets and creatures of every kind. Réka Bucsi invites us to witness this transformative happiness and its secrets.

An empty zoo, a mattress shop, a gas station – in all these strange non-places, pigeons, snails and moles sing of their own worries, problems and crises, unable to perceive the world collapsing around them … An accident in the labs of CERN, the European Organisation for Nuclear Research, extinguishes the last glimmer of hope, thanks to Niki Lindroth von Bahr.

Jerry Stoll follows the preparation and organisation of Vietnam Day, a peaceful protest march from the University of California’s campus in Berkeley to the Oakland Army Terminal, one of the US Army’s major supply ports for the war in Vietnam. The vibrant, carefully photographed film makes the short phase tangible in which the US public was still largely unaware of what was going on in Vietnam and when the shock at the first images and witness reports was just beginning to dawn. While “Sons and Daughters” became a powerful tool of mobilisation at the time, not even its exclusive soundtrack featuring songs by The Grateful Dead, Jon Hendricks and Virgil Gonsalves could prevent it from sinking more or less into oblivion.

A student in Incheon leads a solitary existence, sending off essays late at night, leaving her cramped apartment to smoke out on the street, scrolling through old ads on the internet. When she clicks on an MPEG file that happens to be on her USB stick, a conversation with her grandparents blares forth, recounting their life in the same neighbourhood where she now lives. Once released, their voices won’t stay quiet, creeping into her daily routine and her dreams. As they talk of prejudice against North Korean refugees, taking cardboard from the US military base to build a makeshift house overnight or making malt taffy to earn a living, their endeavours come to life in stop-motion sequences that appear, like them, to belong to a different era. But this is just one of many different visual ideas and animation techniques on display, including hand-drawn sequences of various kinds, scanned-in images that recreate the neighbourhood in cannily imperfect 3D, real photographs and live-action scenes that even show the people behind the voices at one point. History never stays silent; here we see all its overlapping layers.

aw: Silver Dove Short Film International Competition Documentary Film
ap.sel: Officially selected (section: International Competition Documentary Film)

films.t: Sun Ra’s Calling Planet Earth with the OVC
films.syn: Bill Sebastian’s Outer Space Visual Communicator (OVC) was constructed from lights, mirrors and projectors, as well as video effect and mixing equipment. It could be played like a live instrument with hands, feet and even the mouth! Here, we get a glimpse of the OVC’s kaleidoscope visual effects, which were used by the Sun Ra Arkestra to “visualise soundwaves” as part of their touring cosmic stage show.

At the age of just 19, Dan Drasin created “Sunday”, a famous example of American direct cinema: On 9 April 1961, hundreds of folk musicians gathered in New York’s Washington Square Park to protest against the non-renewal of their performance permit. Until then, the park had been a centre of the Beat scene, but now the police used violence against the young musicians – the square was cleared, arrests were made. Drasin’s 16mm camera is in the thick of it, weaving nimbly through the crowd, singling out individuals. This makes “Sunday”, which was co-produced and distributed by the committed left-wing documentarist Emile de Antonio, an early document of a decade marked by massive protests in the US.

Even after more than a century, the poetry of this film is overwhelming. Viking Eggeling, who had already designed so-called scroll paintings with his friend Hans Richter in the 1910s – up to 15-metre-long drawings to be read from left to right showing shapes in transformation –, now takes the logical next step of changing his medium to set the delicate graphic elements in motion.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Hommage: Punto y Raya)

films.syn: 47 animated sketches of a surreal world: a fur collar made of a living wolf; a sawn-off tree that soars to the sky like a balloon; a cat that grows by purring and finally begins to stroke her owner. Réka Bucsi weaves an unpredictable web of fantasies that question human relationships with nature, animals and the cosmos and reduce them to absurdity.

What starts as a harmless production commission evolves into one of the biggest media art debates of recent years: Danish conceptual artist Jens Haaning is asked to reconstruct two of his earlier works for the Museum Kunsten in Aalborg – frames filled with banknotes symbolising the average annual salary in Denmark and Austria. The banknotes, worth half a million kroner or 74,000 euros, are provided by the museum. But, not for the first time, Haaning is annoyed at the working conditions of his profession. He keeps the borrowed money and delivers empty canvases and a title: “Take the Money and Run”. Ole Juncker’s film accompanies the artist in the period following this action – between international media hype, a civil lawsuit by the defrauded institution and personal crises. Haaning, who suffers from bipolar disorder, takes impulsive decisions, invests in real estate and finds himself in financial straits which he seeks to offset by ad hoc sales of his work. The pressure on the protagonist is mirrored in a rapid montage of disparate images: car rides, surreal animations, action cam footage of a parkour runner and TV reports condense into a portrait of the artist as a rogue who is determined to explore whether art, at least, can get away with crime.

On 9 September 1971, a prison riot broke out at Attica State Prison, New York, which was brutally suppressed by the National Guard after four days, resulting in the deaths of 43 people. “Teach Our Children” sides passionately with the rebellious prison inmates and investigates the inhumane conditions that provoked the revolt. The statements of the inmates recorded on film denounce the open racism of the prison system and the exploitation in the form of work measures. On the other side is the “clear conscience” of those who gave the order to shoot, first among them prison warden Oswald: “Do you have any sense of guilt at all?” – “No.”

It sprawls, cracks, bursts: The balcony of two flatmates is slowly but steadily overgrown by a red climbing plant with evil-looking tubers. And our flatmates? Sit in the middle, stoically smoking, ignoring the bursting windows behind them. There was a funny rain – but not water. With this poignant and charged one-take idea and beautifully realistic character design, Stella Hood examines the dilemma of the eternal spectator: Here are two figures who register that there is something fundamentally wrong with the world but simply continue with their daily routines. Who neither get worked up nor wonder nor take action. And whose lethargy is hilarious, not least because it is an uncomfortable reminder of our own inaction. What global crisis could the two be ignoring so nonchalantly? Stella Hood leaves this open, even though the plants make climate change an obvious choice. In any case, a parcel delivery is expected. Have a look downstairs? Sure, “but not today.” “Nah, not today,” the other one replies. “Perhaps tomorrow, we’ll see.”

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: International Competition Animated Film)

films.syn: In the evening of 9 February 2022, four young men sit around a table in Kyiv. The friends are discussing the situation: 120,000 Russian soldiers are stationed right at the Ukrainian border. What is going to happen? In “The Birds Are Silent”, director and cinematographer Leo Dzhyshyashvili captures an equally private and historical moment. What is striking is the clarity with which Andriy, Olexandr, Ivan and Sasha assess the consequences of the imminent attack: Potential decisions about their own future are mixed with concerns about relatives and the bewilderment at being thrown into a situation that provokes both helplessness and disgust. But there is a glimmer of hope – perhaps the imagined horror scenarios are nothing but a waste of energy? Cut. Some of the debaters have become soldiers; one has barricaded himself in the bathroom with a narrow mattress and a meal. Within eight minutes, Dzhyshyashvili has tied together a before and after that make you shudder.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Panorama: Central and Eastern Europe)

films.syn: What happens in a person permanently trapped in the destructive loneliness of constant self-comparison? How does a person who fools others with neoliberal dreams just so they do not have to give up their own feel? This bittersweet, cheerfully tense musical by Niki Lindroth von Bahr pulls us into the masked nervousness of modern society with humour, singing and dancing.

In 1974, the Maternity Center, located in a low-income Chicago neighbourhood, is acutely threatened by lack of financing from its funding body, North Western University. Resistance begins to form in the predominantly Black community, since this is an institution with a 75-year-old history that has provided countless woman with safe and affordable home-births. “The Chicago Maternity Center Story” uses this civil protest as a starting point to tell the story of the rampant commercialisation of medical care in the USA, including its sexist and racist connotations. A film that approaches the issue sometimes gently, sometimes with agitprop vigour.

Can a geometric structure be seductive? The answer of this spare and yet utterly charming film is clear: Yes, it can! A simple white line on a black background bewitches us with its dynamic curves as we marvel, open-mouthed, at its suppleness and excellent timing. This line is a saucy star that would be a credit to every burlesque show.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Hommage: Punto y Raya)

films.syn: Step into 9-year-old Juniper’s world as she navigates complicated memories and guilt related to Magnolia, a woman who comes to work for the family. In misleadingly delicate animation and tone, “The Dollhouse” positions home as the workshop where unjust power dynamics are formed. The story unfolds in all directions, at times offering specific interactions.

The digital shapes growing into the sky in this video artwork are reminiscent of Chinese ink landscapes. They strive upwards, like the sound which seems to pull them up by invisible threads. Everything is steeped in acetic colours that lift the landscape out of the human realm. A journey to a strange and yet familiar world.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Hommage: Punto y Raya)

films.ot: Sonades de la calor del foc
films.syn: This rhythm-driven animation is inspired by the 4th movement of the “Sonades de la calor del foc,” the “Sonatas of the Heat of the Fire”, created in 1984 by Catalan composer Josep Maria Mestres Quadreny. It passes through four poeticised spaces: The first is dominated by coloured blocs, the second by gravity, the third by silence, and the fourth takes us back to vibrant life at last.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Hommage: Punto y Raya)

films.t: The German Democratic Republic – A Land of Books [excerpt]
films.ot: Deutsche Demokratische Republik – Ein Land der Bücher [Ausschnitt]
films.syn: The well-known illustrator Werner Klemke uses his drawings to teach the youngest bookworms about the value of reading. Taking this as a starting point, Lotte Thiel presents the GDR as a land of books whose capital is Leipzig. Figures and images from the 1971 International Book Art Exhibition underscore the significance accorded to books as a tool for shaping the “socialist personality”.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Matinee Saxon State Archive)

films.t: The Good Fight: The Abraham Lincoln Brigade in the Spanish Civil War
films.syn: In life, people do things they are proud of, and others they are not proud of – but it is impossible not to be proud of having participated in the Spanish Civil War (1936–1939), even if the Spanish Republic and its alliance of International Brigades lost. This is one of the American veterans whose war memories – bitter, but marked by self-respect – are honoured by this film. The Abraham Lincoln Brigade consisted of US volunteers who fought against Spanish and German fascism and for democracy under adverse conditions and without party affiliations until 1939, while the US government pursued a strict and ultimately fatal policy of appeasement. A refreshingly undogmatic document with a wealth of fresh archive material.

films.t: The Great History of Western Philosophy
films.ot: La gran historia de la filosofía occidental
films.syn: “Do not attempt to reason with this movie. It is raving mad and makes no sense at all.” Aria Covamonas places this announcement right at the start of this wild cutout animation ride through Chinese and Western history (of philosophy) – and keeps their word. Countless figures appear in seemingly arbitrary order who, with no discernible common thread, condemn to death, argue or flirt – but do it in the most absurd and funny way. At one point, for example, Plato appears, who must be bathed by the elephants because he spent too much time in his cave. But Mao, Mickey Mouse, Nietzsche and Lacan also make appearances. They are all taken from the public domain, as are the Chinese dialogues which issue from their mouths, edited by rhythm; the English subtitles have nothing to do with them. According to Covamonas, any interpretation is possible – and welcome. Nonetheless, themes begin to emerge: The arbitrary use of violence that characterises every authoritarian regime is lampooned, and so is the absurdity of every canon. But Covamonas, too, is influenced by it: A visual homage to Dadaistic collage art à la Hannah Höch, an acoustic reference to the noise of early sound films, this exuberant treasure-trove of sampled global culture can be thoroughly enjoyed and invites us to discover references while drifting through it.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: International Competition Animated Film)

films.syn: A tinted nitrate fragment of the company film “A. Gutberlet & Co., Leipzig-Mölkau, Spezialfabrik für Falzmaschinen und Faden-Buchheftmaschinen, gegründet 1901“ (specialist in the manufacture of folding machines and thread book stitching machines, established 1901) was an exceptional find. It could be restored in its original colour tones by analogue methods in 2024 and then digitised. Combined with the dupe negative of another version, it now offers insights into the factory halls and the work on the machines.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Matinee Saxon State Archive)

films.syn: A cinematic daydream in corrugated cardboard and paint, shot with a Super8 camera. The soundscape consists of hills, some easily climbed, others requiring the last ounce of strength. The shapes, colouring, cross-fades and rhythms of this encounter with paper also shift between tough and tender and are made tangible both on the visual and the tonal level.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Hommage: Punto y Raya)

films.syn: Grandfather’s hands making pottery, the vertical linearity of a tower, a train crashing into a car – all of these are fragile, newly born film sketches that crowd each other out in a survival game for the filmmaker’s attention. The sceneries fight against each other, intertwine to form new strands, sink into an endless flood of information, shatter in a sea of open browser tabs. With his authentic voice-over and a mesmerising collection of moving images, director Konstantin von Sichart’s alter ego offers us a deep insight into his creative process. Marked by his neurodivergence, he learns before our eyes to cope with his inability to concentrate on one thing – and to weave meaning from these strands, remain true to his film idea. But how can this ever result in a film? Toxically coloured images, naively drawn and finely crafted, AI-generated, filmed from a monitor, collaged, worked-on – a wealth of tools and aesthetic approaches translates the described mental overload into the language of design. The film thus becomes more than a self-reflection of modern filmmaking: It is the portrait of a new generation – caught between the compulsion to take everything in and have a position on everything and the urge to stand still or even run away.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: International Competition Animated Film)

films.syn: In the beginning, humans seem so very far away, the only sign of them the twinkling lights of Montreal on the horizon across the water. Deslauriers Island is home to one of largest colonies of ring-billed gulls in the world, and initially it feels like a realm for them alone: a whole legion of elegant white birds gathered together on the grass, flapping, crouching, calling, mating, the camera right in their midst, right down at their level, seeing as they do. But this non-human utopia is evoked in order to be progressively undermined, as markers are placed in the ground, traps set and specimens captured. Some will be released with leg rings or daubed-on markings, but others won’t be so lucky. The sky over the landfill site is thick with beating wings and when the beaks screech as one, the sound is deafening. No wonder the voice on the radio says they’re losing control, although that hardly justifies the solution they find. Birds hunt birds in the wild, but there’s something particularly savage about seeing it be guided by human hand. At the beginning of the 20th century, the ring-billed gull was nearly hunted to extinction, but their life circle continues unabated here – who can blame nature for finding a way? Yet the stakes are different now, and the old laws no longer apply. Will the meek still inherit the earth?

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: International Competition Documentary Film)

films.syn: In her second feature-length film, Lee Anne Schmitt leaves California behind to explore the disparate influences that have shaped life in Utah’s Henry Mountains, home to one of the country’s last remaining bison herds, which are hunted to this day. Hewing closer to pure observation than much of the rest of her work, Schmitt and her roving camera stick tightly to the everyday rhythms of the contemporary cowboys who organise these now touristic hunts. The images of buffalos being shot at close range, disembowelled or stuffed speak for themselves, as do the endless landscapes, stubborn iconography of the former Wild West and the story of the Native American dream recounted in voice-over: the impossible return to a land never again empty.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Hommage: Lee Anne Schmitt)

films.t: The Lions by the River Tigris
films.syn: “It’s nice here, let’s play,” says Fakhri, holding a small loudspeaker for Fadil, the violinist. But there is no audience. The two men are standing in the ruins of Mosul. Three years of occupation by the Islamic State terrorist militia have left the old town almost completely destroyed. Along with the buildings, the 8,000-year history and culture of the second-largest Iraqi city seemed to have been wiped out forever. Life returns slowly. Art treasures are being restored, there are theatres, music again, and Fakhri’s small private museum where he collects anything he can lay his hands on: wooden doors, bronze figures, soap from1910, a ventilator. He has already amassed 7,000 exhibits and is especially fond of an ancient portal with two lions. Damaged, but perhaps still salvageable, it sits enthroned in the ruins of Bashar’s parents’ house like a peace time relic. Bashar visits it almost daily, hoping that reconstruction is possible. But Fakhri turns out to drive a hard bargain – he wants this portal at all costs … With a steady hand, Kurdish-Norwegian director Zaradasht Ahmed tells a deeply human story, intertwining the darkest and lightest side of the species: the mania of destruction and the strength to go on.

We have all been there: A noise escapes in the bus, followed by an unpleasant smell – and everyone knows where it came from. But why are farts so embarrassing? At least that is what fart star Pongy Pippa wonders. She dances with tubas and trumpets in time with our digestion to show how much work and skill goes into making such sounds. A musical show for the most human of noises.

films.t: The Most Beautiful in the World – Books of Today: International Book Art Exhibition Leipzig 1971 [excerpt]
films.ot: Die Schönsten der Welt – Bücher von heute: Internationale Buchkunst-Ausstellung Leipzig 1971 [Ausschnitt]
films.syn: Commissioned by the German Book Traders’ Association, Lotte Thiel follows the preparations for the 1971 International Book Art Exhibition, prominently supported on screen and on the soundtrack. The tradition of this fair is recalled, from its predecessor BUGRA 1914 to the first IBA in 1927 and the subsequent events that took place every five to six years starting in 1959. Award-winning illustrations can be viewed in detail.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Matinee Saxon State Archive)

films.t: The Pool or Death of a Goldfish
films.syn: A fishing hook pierces the lips of a lonely swimmer. Shortly afterwards, the young woman finds herself served up on a bed of salads, shrunk to the size of a goldfish and being carved up piece by piece under the critical eyes of two gourmets. Despite the pain she remains submissive, wishes them bon appétit and warns wistfully: “I don’t know if I will fulfil your wishes in your bellies.” Soon the swimmer will turn out to be the daughter of the two gourmets; the bittersweet, macabre opening one of many variations on the dilemma of unfulfillable parental expectations. The unsaid and suppressed dominate the artfully interleaved stop motion images that navigate fluidly through phantasies and memories. Time and again, they take the form of water: Puddles become brooks become swimming pools. And the question of one’s identity is decided at the edge of the pool.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Panorama: Central and Eastern Europe)

films.syn: Two pieces of news change director Caroline Guimbal’s life at Christmas: Her mother Natalie has cancer and she herself is pregnant. She follows Natalie over a period of two years, entering into a dialogue that extends across several levels. On the one hand, Guimbal films her mother in close, delicate shots, listens to her memories, documents her close connection with nature and the gradual decline caused by the disease. Another conversation is conducted offscreen, a conversation with herself that recounts experienced brutality and abuse: It is about all the men who beat up and exploited her mother and who have also left their mark on the daughter’s childhood and adolescent memories, not least on the recurring pattern of her own relationships. “The Red Moon Eclipse” is a bitterly sensitive portrait that examines the conditions and simultaneity of events. Like a blood moon, which describes a total eclipse of the sun where sun, moon and earth are aligned, Caroline Guimbal draws lines: between mother and mother, daughter and mother, past and present. What is left at the end is the question of love – true love and love that only pretends to be true and usually causes pain.

aw: Prize of the International Film Critics (FIPRESCI Prize)
ap.sel: Officially selected (section: International Competition Documentary Film)

films.syn: Mathilde’s home is a hive of activity: Mama is getting ready in the bathroom, and Papa is baking a cake. Guests are expected for dinner. Mathilde is supposed to help with the preparations, too. The living room has to be tidied up because her toy cars are scattered everywhere. How lucky that there are two little friends who turn tidying up into a fast-paced car race.

The figures in this experimental short film for cinema greenhorns seem to be spinning on a turntable. Houses, plants, birds, and a face pass before our eyes. To a lively tune, blossoms unfold, eggs and chicks fly, the sun goes up and down, until everything starts all over again. A small, tongue-in-cheek story that also tells of the early days of animation.

A map of Europe is marked with numbers, their values rising from south to north, east to west. These are the gross minimum wages of each nation – 281 euros in Bosnia and Herzegovina, 842 euros in Slovenia, 1,498 euros in Germany and 1,613 euros in Ireland. Director Srđan Kovačević is committed to transparency. But he is not the only one: The office of workers’ rights “Delavska svetovalnica” in Slovenian Ljubljana bases its activities on enlightenment and transparency. It is approached by workers who are exploited and cheated by companies, who get neither employment contracts nor wages. Many of them do not have Slovenian citizenship, and a legal situation fraught with pitfalls makes them vulnerable and mute. Goran Zrnić, a former electrician turned lawyer, Goran Lukić, staunch union activist, and social worker Laura Orel raise their voices for them, counsel amid piles of paper and permanently ringing phones. Kovačević’s camera matches the speed of the dynamic situation and captures the well-nigh incredible. “The Thing to Be Done” brings together moments of exhaustion and triumph, making us angry and hopeful in turns, combining direct cinema and class struggle into an, in the best sense, inflammatory power.

aw: Prize of the Interreligious Jury
ap.sel: Officially selected (section: International Competition Documentary Film)

films.syn: In this early short, Lee Anne Schmitt and Lee Lynch craft an ambling, quietly profound portrait of a place quite literally close to home: the so-called Wash, a strip of wasteland by the Santa Clara River that backs on to Newhall, California, where the two directors lived at the time. As the duo take turns explaining in voice-over, this in-between space is used by and home to a diverse group of local residents, a balance that is quickly upset once the adjacent hills are turned into an upmarket housing estate. As the natural and the urban blur together, the mood turns pensive. Nostalgia can be felt for even the most unremarkable of settings.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Hommage: Lee Anne Schmitt)

films.t: The Woman Who Poked the Leopard
films.syn: When Stella Nyanzi enters a room, action is guaranteed. The Ugandan feminist, gender researcher, anthropologist and poet does not mince her words in her fight against state oppression. She went to prison in 2017 for a vulgar poem in which she ridiculed head of state Yoweri Museveni, who has been in office for almost 40 years. After she was released, Nyanzi ran for Parliament without the necessary funds for a campaign, printing and distributing posters and flyers in the slums of Kampala with her children. Her daughter did her mother’s make-up and hair for public appearances. Sometimes her almost adult children longed for more time for themselves. The family repeatedly faced police violence and finally emigrated to Germany. Using a mobile handheld camera, the film absorbs its protagonist’s power, its rhythm matching her angry lyrics. The result is the portrait of a woman who has made radicalism and provocation her way of life. We get to know an activist who permanently pushes herself and the people around her to the limits. Still, it is hard not to get infected by Stella Nyanzi’s energy.

aw: DEFA Sponsoring Prize
ver.di Prize for Solidarity, Humanity and Fairness
ap.sel: Officially selected (section: German Competition Documentary Film)

films.syn: As a philosopher, Frenchman Bruno Latour (1947–2022) opened not only rooms of reflection but whole houses. An anthropologist and sociologist, he became an internationally renowned advocate for shifting paradigms, with the aim of re-defining the place of the human individual in the cycle of nature. Latour coined the term “ecological class,” to be created on planet earth to become aware of fundamental options for action in crises. But: How do we react to his questions, visions, and concepts in our daily life, far removed from science and philosophy? Do they reach us? Do they spark debates when we encounter them? Raphaël Girardot and Vincent Gaullier found individuals in France, Belgium and Senegal who want to go their own way in observing, describing and changing conditions, or already do so in communities – on fields and in forests, fishing or protesting, as autonomous beings or in familiar structures. The directors confront some of them with Latour’s writings, trigger thoughts and conversations and let Bruno Latour himself guide us through the episodes in short interview sequences from the internet. Increasingly marked by his cancer, he shows himself to be a precise analyst with verve, humour, and clear statements.

When Tord comes home from work one day, he meets an unknown person of the same name in a redesigned apartment. His old home has given way to the new one and is now behind the neighbouring door. The second Tord turns out to be a pleasant conversationalist, a soulmate: A weighty reason not to ask further questions – until they become inevitable.

This film is archival cinema of high jewel-like quality. There is no dialogue, only a quote from Franz Kafka at the beginning: “There is plenty of hope, an infinite amount of hope – but not for us.” The opening shots captivate with a dynamic dance of people and machines: We witness workers assembling locomotives. Soon we find ourselves mingling with the people waiting on the platform in their old-fashioned hats and coats, later admiring the idyllic landscapes behind the carriage windows and sensing that for some of our fellow passengers, this journey must have felt like an expedition into space. Then soldiers fill the images, streams of soldiers on their way to the First World War. Weapons are being transported, many weapons. They are manufactured in factories. The ghost of war wanders through Europe. This feeling occupies the film and points beyond it. What is stored in the archive material – uniform caps and top hats, victims and perpetrators, luxury and misery, cattle and command carriages, Hitler and Chaplin – has a connection to the present, even to the future. Whether we can hope for it depends on how well we remember the lessons of history.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Panorama: Central and Eastern Europe)

films.syn: A black-and-white range of shapes and gradient colour saturations demonstrates the possibilities of the digital image. This visual narrative treats the screen as a space that exists parallel to the physical world, inviting us to explore an unreal three-dimensional universe whose depths are amplified by Tim Prebble’s ambient soundtrack.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Hommage: Punto y Raya)

films.syn: The programmatic sub-header of this film is “a black & white movie”. In “Trick Bag”, young people from a variety of origins talk about peer pressure and power struggles in Chicago neighbourhoods that used to be regarded as ethnically homogenous but are now centres of many cultures. Whites, Blacks, Latinos and Latinas appear on camera. They are Vietnam veterans, gang members and factory workers who try to organise peaceful coexistence. Instead of fighting each other, the tenor goes, they should all become aware of their situation as segregated and precariously employed. An entertaining and feistily presented plea for solidarity and coexistence in Chicago – representative of many American metropolises of that time.

Kate Hyndman, Stella Nowicki and Sylvia Woods talk on camera about their eventful past as union women in the 1930s and 1940s. They worked at the grassroots at the time of the Great Depression and global crises and helped establish the US-American union movement in the first place. Vividly and full of verve, they describe the precarious working and living conditions they experienced first-hand, but also the democratic spirit and the solidarity that shaped them and their union comrades. The filmmakers add contemporary photo and moving image sequences to this captivating political oral history – a rich and, in terms of film history, influential treasure trove of left-wing America.

Grainy black and white images alternate with overexposed colour shots. Dreamy tracking shots through barren, rocky landscapes, flying with griffon vultures and storks, follow static shots by a flowing brook or near a grasshopper on a stone. Close-ups of grasses, insects, seemingly accidentally discovered stone sculptures, then a series of interior views of a slightly dilapidated villa in the country. Scenes of a baptism, at the end overlapping details of a campfire. One could describe countless such impressions, one wants to keep circling with the birds forever, roaming through the rocks, lingering in the community … Ewelina Rosińska spent a few years travelling through Portugal with photographer Nuno Barroso and a 16mm camera, occasionally accompanied by artists and eco-activists, capturing landscapes, encounters and places. Composed with dreamlike certainty in a captivating and supple rhythm, her film is like a visual poem about the ambivalence of human presence in nature.

Almost 100,000 people follow Bahati Ngazi on her eponymous TikTok channel. This is where the well-known radio host presents herself, pushes Mombasa’s small businesses and promotes herself as the woman with the “money complexion” who regularly bathes in fresh coconut milk. Her latest idea: She wants the local sex gurus – wise women from the Swahili community – to teach her a range of practices and thus mature from a novice (mikleso) to an expert (kungwi). The evening before already turns into a ritual: Bahati and a friend achieve a state of ecstasy with a bunch of khat leaves, sweets, tea, and music. Director Saitabao Kaiyare becomes an interested and complicit companion on this educational journey, repeatedly directing his focus on feminist issues that are also on Bahati’s mind, not least in her radio show: What demands are made on Kenyan women? And is there a “love education” for men? “Unyagoni: Bahati’s Sex Education Journey” is the portrait of a bold and vibrant woman who shares not only her self-confidence but also her occasional insecurities. An entertaining yet no less complex journey.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: International Competition Documentary Film)

films.syn: When we consider the relationship between the real world and its representation on maps, we cannot help but notice that people tend to overestimate their shaping influence. Just because a phenomenon is represented in a very simplified form in cartography, its complexity in the real world does not diminish. And just because we erase a river, for example, from the map, even contain it and build over it in the real world, it has not disappeared. It has just become invisible. Anna-Maria Dutoit roams the urban landscape of Montreal in search of the water veins that were once a feature of this area. Centuries of settlement and urbanization have polluted, buried, and shifted them underground. Only circling seagulls and manhole covers remind us of what lies below. Guided by some of the oldest maps of Montreal, “Vanished Past” follows the forgotten rivers of the megalopolis and explores – accompanied by a sometimes burbling, sometimes splashing soundtrack – the unique aquatic universes that unfold in its hideaways. A cursory glance may find that the element of water no longer seems to play a role in the concrete urban landscape. At least until heavy rain pours down, flooding the streets – and reminding the city of its supposedly vanished past.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: German Competition Documentary Film)

films.syn: A study on texture, amorphous forms and the body via image processing and video synthesis. Starting as a simple exercise in contrast and keying effects, the electronic eye of the video camera begins to hallucinate more and more as it tracks the artist through a series of oblique experiments, before finally breaking down completely, recreating reality as a vibrating electronic mesh.

A train ride into abstraction created with increasingly abstract AI-generated imagery, this film is a simple yet mesmerising gesture which explores the essentials of the digital image. Hypnotic and thoroughly immersive, the experience highlights AI images as more than replicas of reality, but rather as abstract and architectural structures to explore.

Katya lights the candles on her 22nd birthday cake alone, nobody is there yet to celebrate with her. She has recently moved in with her mother. Mama drinks and has just had a new baby: Amina. Abandoned as a child, Katya grew up without her mother, who lost custody because of her alcohol addiction. Now Katya frequently takes care of her little sister while her mother is nowhere to be found. She always returns with professions of guilt and promises to do better. Katya finds support in her friend Tanya, with whom she shares a similar biography. And she finds recognition in her job as a welder, for which she has a particular talent. In “Welded Together”, Anastasiya Miroshnichenko portrays a young woman who clings for a long time to the idea of a family that can be put back together, even though there is a lot of evidence to the contrary. Miroshnichenko mainly captures her protagonist through her facial expressions – Katya’s usually shifts between emptiness and sadness; it is like a mirror that reveals the complexity and tragedy of the situation. Meanwhile, the social services department is responsible for protecting Katya and Amina. The office becomes an ambivalent place to go in the midst of this equally dark and fateful winter.

aw: MDR Film Prize

films.syn: A mud volcano in Akhtala, Georgia, constantly produces material for the local spa industry: Heated and spread on large linen cloths, the shimmering grey goo is believed to heal the sick. But not only the guests roam the bathhouse, but also five-year-old Tako in her summer dress, who is afraid of the so-called Mud Man. The place and its volcano are shrouded in legends – how much truth is behind them? Tako discusses this and other things with her grandmother, whose job it is to wash the used linen cloths and hang them up to dry in the sun. Together they animate this unadorned post-Soviet era building filled with constant spluttering and dripping, while a blubbering sound seems to be coming from the mud pit. Is the mud really whispering?

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Panorama: Central and Eastern Europe)

films.t: Where Did You Get That Woman?
films.syn: Despite many hardships and misfortunes, Joan Williams radiates an infectious zest for life. The seventy-year-old works as a cleaner in the washrooms of a high-class Chicago night club. When it closes at the end of the 1970s, her professional biography also ends – involuntarily, because Joan liked her job. After all, it brought her into contact with the showbiz and glamour of the city. Set against the glittering backdrop of downtown Chicago, “Where Did You Get That Woman?” uses an individual’s story to explore class antagonisms, race relations and the difficulties of relationships and getting older. Last but not least, the film also discovers in Williams’ story the long history of African-American migration from the segregated South to the supposedly more liberal North of the United States.

The old shots smell like phenol and brown coal dust. In the spring of 1991, two documentary filmmakers travelled through the former energy triangle of the GDR, centred around the towns of Spremberg, Hoyerswerda and Schwarze Pumpe. In the midst of despair and resignation, they demanded analyses. Those who faced layoffs answered: “When there’s no work, there’s no work.” Or more simply: “Bang, out, gone, that’s it.” Thirty years later, Martin Gressmann and the documentarists from 1991 are not done yet with the fractures and open wounds of the industry liquidations right after reunification. The comparison between the history – full of murky air and people who hide from the camera – and the apparently appeased present does not lend itself to make-overs; the landscapes that followed brown coal mining are not pretty yet, the river Spree is only halfway cleaned-up, the power plant is still one of the main CO2 emitters in Europe. You often have to look twice to understand that an important leap in time was made in the images. The dirt and the energy of the past keep coming back, and Lusatia continues to “serve and work” in the “subconscious of the distant capital”. Idiosyncratic texts and bold documentary manoeuvres generate an ambivalent mix of surfaces and deep strata, erosion and repair of an industrial landscape.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: German Competition Documentary Film)

films.syn: In August 1975, 80,000 coal miners in the Appalachians laid down tools for several weeks in a so-called wildcat strike, that is, a labour dispute organised without unions. They went on strike for the right to strike in the first place, which until then had been de facto taken from them by dubious contracts. The film team is in the thick of the dynamic events, filming spontaneous and prepared speeches, interviewing strikers, recording strike songs by left-wing folk musicians who perform in the crowd. A film about speech and speechlessness, solidarity and social injustice.

films.t: Witness to War: Dr. Charlie Clements
films.syn: Based on the book “Witness to War: An American Doctor in El Salvador”, the film, which won awards both at the Oscars and in Leipzig, tells the story of the deeply religious Vietnam veteran Charlie Clements. The son of a military family, he first embarked on a career as a high-ranking soldier and flew numerous supply missions in the Vietnam War, only to finally make a radical turn. In 1970, he refused to serve, was discharged from the Air Force and studied medicine. In the early 1980s, he ended up on the side of the guerrilla in El Salvador, one of the “new Vietnams” of interventionist US foreign policy, as contemporary critics put it. The film is about how both wars reverberated back in the United States.

A woman drives home by night and feels another woman watching her, a brief story at once opaque and ominous told first via intertitles before being partially repeated in voice-over. 16mm shots of a city by night, shop fronts, highways, street lights passing in a blur, muted traffic noise, snatches of music, the sound of crickets. Lee Anne Schmitt’s mysterious miniature draws a line between two women and a trauma they seemingly share. Undefined yet no less deeply felt, it remains as hard to fully parse as the horses riding over a prairie in grainy black and white or the figure in a dress lying on the side of a road, stretched out in the sunshine and leaves.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Hommage: Lee Anne Schmitt)

films.syn: Behind the bark of a tree, a clever little bark beetle girl lives with her colony. But people put the forest idyll at risk. After a major fire, she finds refuge in a school. Scared at first, she slowly learns to communicate with humans and finds her way back home with the help of new friends. A short ode to learning.

films.t: Writing Life: Annie Ernaux Through the Eyes of High School Students
films.ot: Écrire la vie – Annie Ernaux racontée par des lycéennes et des lycéens
films.syn: Like her previous film, “Elementary”, Claire Simon’s latest work pays homage to the educational process, once again opening the doors of school classrooms. This time, texts by Annie Ernaux – a French feminist, writer and Nobel Prize winner – are on the curriculum. Ernaux describes her concept of autosociobiography as “writing life, not mine, nor theirs, nor even one in particular. Life with situations that we all go through, but that we, as individuals, experience differently. Body image, education, the sense of belonging, sexual condition, social trajectory, the existence of others, disease, grief. […] I did not try to write about myself, to write a book about my life. I made use of my life, of the general, ordinary events of my life, of the situations and feelings I have experienced. As if it were material I needed to explore to grasp and uncover some kind of perceptible truth.” The teachers create smart frameworks for discussions filled with freedom and dynamics, where the young people reveal themselves in all their beauty and vulnerability, extrapolating the author’s experiences to their own lives. And this is when Claire Simon’s “writing life camera” documents charming moments of how Ernaux’s texts empower and inspire them, as they passionately delve into her words.

The activist in her awakened at an early age. Even as an adolescent, Juma Xipaia felt that she would dedicate herself to her Indigenous people’s fight for the right to exist in the Brazilian Amazon region. For the Amazon is their mother, the knowledge, and the cure. More than ten years later, Juma knows what it really means to be an activist. As the first female chief of the Middle Xingu region, she has survived assassination attempts, experienced state violence against protesters, must discover illegal prospectors who are clearing the forests and poisoning the soil and the rivers. But the 34-year-old also sees hope emerge for the Indigenous people of Brazil, because the 2023 change of government gave them their own Ministry for the first time. Juma becomes an undersecretary of state and has her second child: Yanuni. The Austrian Richard Ladkani portrays Juma Xipaia and her husband Hugo, a special investigator working for the environmental authorities, after they let him accompany their daily life for several years. Ladkani mixes fascinating landscape shots with the explosive power of “embedded journalism”, using the full potential of the big screen in one moment and intensifying intimate moment in the next. The result is private and personal, poetic and political. Above all, the film transports Juma Xipaia’s message that despite every disappointment, responsibility for one’s life should not be placed in the hands of others but kept close to home.

Looking around with her stepfather. Gentle hills, low vegetation, dry soil, ruins of houses from the 1970s. Ali Ekber Vural once left for Germany from here. At the time he buried his binoculars with the Zeiss lenses and never found them again. Now his stepdaughter’s camera takes a close look. Dêrsim – a name that has disappeared from the map of Turkey, yet still lives on in many people’s memories. The region, a former refuge for Kurds and Alevis, was renamed “Tunceli” in 1935 as part of a national homogenisation process. This landscape has witnessed state violence, forced resettlements, massacres, torture, assimilation policies, and a lack of coming to terms with all this. “Can you imagine such a man coming from this environment and integrating in Germany?” Ali asks. A narrated summary of his life that starts with the whispered, forbidden language of his childhood and leads to the complex diaspora experience in the new homeland, where, to put it bluntly, he was left high and dry. You have to have been there to understand what happened. Maybe a new, shared view will be possible then.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: German Competition Documentary Film)

films.syn: In 1965, the longest farm workers’ strike in US-American history unrolled in Delano, California. Led by Cesar Chavez, the as yet unorganised Mexican seasonal labourers fought successfully for better working conditions and the right to found a union of their own, the National Farm Workers Association (NFWA). “¡Huelga!” is the partisan portrait of an emerging solidarity group that not only stood up against the unregulated capitalism in the agricultural sector but also declared war on the racism of the white landowners. In addition to depicting the mechanisms of the strike, the mobile camera also makes a point of documenting the degrading living conditions of the people who kept one of the most powerful industries in the country going.

First we hear a crackling sound, then a diffuse orange light glows in the darkness. A siren growing louder and the sound of a helicopter instantly mark the scene as a place of danger. There is a fire. First in the distance, a moment later everywhere. Trees and palms go up in flames. The fire’s power is immense. The firefighters and everyone else who is fighting the wildfires around Los Angeles act with remarkable calm. Nobody is running, the communication chain is working smoothly, TV reporters are broadcasting live, helpers are setting up emergency shelters, taking care of injured animals, cutting fire lines in front of neighbours’ homes. A tried-and-tested routine, efficiency and a great willingness to help. The crisis seems to bring out the best in the people. This uncommented observation is also a tribute to their commitment. But the longer it goes on, the more the question arises why solidarity and sustainable action seem to work in emergencies, while it seems impossible to tackle the crisis before it becomes an inferno. The film’s cinematic meditation on pyropolitics takes a look at our age of multiple crises. The permanent global fire management makes it easy to forget that behind those fires lie geopolitical causes that must be dealt with – not with water, but with political decisions.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: International Competition Documentary Film)

films.syn: Gandzani, a Georgian village close to the Armenian border. Friends since childhood, three young men from this largely Armenian community are gradually beginning to take different life paths: Henrikh is about to start studying in the capital. He’s worried about the Georgian government’s close ties to Russia, but he’s willing to take serious risks for his political ideals. Karlen, on the other hand, is dissatisfied with life as a shepherd, longs for the ideals of the Soviet Union and plans to go to Moscow as an immigrant worker. And Hakob has to rethink his role in the community when his long-distance relationship starts to crumble. In this airy, sensuous coming-of-age meditation, Marlene Edoyan creates a fitting space to show the period of upheaval between the spirit of the new, resignation and melancholy.

A queer auto-narrative about longing in three acts that addresses seemingly chaotic but systemically functioning cycles of attraction and revulsion, fear and desire, consumption and withdrawal, ecstasy and regret. While the film creates a timeless immediacy, the first-person narrator's commentary, in contrast, sounds like overthinking rather than an unquestioned moment of just-being-there. Whether at the club, by the lake or in the student cafeteria – one’s own judgement is always quicker than the question of how one is actually doing at that moment. But gradually something begins to change: An initially barely perceptible frequency shift sets in. The fragmented staccato of the first comments gradually gives way to a tale that gently settles in the interstices between dune, dream and reality.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: German Competition Documentary Film)

films.syn: Prague-based filmmaker Helena Třeštíková has been filming marriage stories since the early 1980s, resulting in several long-term documentaries. Ivana and Václav’s everlasting marriage covenant is the subject of observation in this episode, which ranges from the day before the wedding to the present day. Back then, in December 1980, Ivana is 21 years old and Václav 24. Both study architecture and marry “because we like each other. And other things. Things better not talked about.” The first child is born shortly after the wedding. Třeštíková is obviously attracted to certain places she keeps returning to, but mostly to people and the way they try to give their lives meaningful directions. In this “Marriage Story”, we discern an incredible desire for expansion and growth which becomes evident in an accumulation of objects, children and responsibilities – one of the underlying motives of the Strnads’ marriage which gradually unfolds over 35 years together.

“My life is a prison”, Adelina says. The young woman is smoking and looking into the camera, her parents sitting on the sofa to her right and left. In black and white and the narrow 4:3 ratio, this family scene feels oppressive: Adeline spent eleven years under house arrest here, with a father who refuses to accept her identity and a mother who seems loving but powerless. In Georgia, there is neither freedom nor security for trans persons like Adelina. Anti-queer attacks happen in broad daylight; the legal situation of the LGBTQ community has recently deteriorated further. When the protagonist at last leaves her parents’ village to go to Vienna, the style of Rati Tsiteladze’s debut film also changes. The lipstick glows red, the lights of the big city neon yellow. A different, freer life seems possible. But the freedom brings new challenges: financial and health problems, communicating in a foreign language – and loneliness. “A Song Without Home” is the intimate, impressionistic long-term portrait of a person who wants to define herself and clings to an unshakeable conviction: “No law can erase who we are.”

Three kids trudge through the snow. One of them sees a falling star and gets to make a wish. But it’s not quite that simple, because the two friends think the childish wish is too short-sighted and selfish in light of global problems. Ninety seconds in bright colours and with cute characters that show briefly and succinctly what goes bitterly wrong when the right thing is no longer right.

Raúl Ruiz was part of the militant cinema movement that put itself in the service of the Chilean Popular Front, but remained an outsider. He employed experiment and irony to dissect social contradictions. In “Abastecimiento”, Ruiz addresses the supply problems under the Unidad Popular government, confronting the views of a woman from a bourgeois background with those of the socialist Minister for Economic Affairs. He follows this with a depiction of the activities of the Juntas de Abastecimiento y Precios (JAP), locally organised committees for the control and just distribution of food and everyday goods. The provocative juxtaposition paints a picture of an impossible dialogue. The film was banned at the time and was believed lost for ages. It was only recently rediscovered. Leipzig was not the place for the feature film director who emigrated to Paris after the military coup, but Ruiz was a frequent guest at the Berlinale Forum.

Through numerous video essays in film and media theory, Kevin B. Lee has played a key role in developing the form of the so-called desktop film. The elegant meta-staging reflects the fact that his digital desktop is research tool, media archive and distribution channel at the same time. Lee’s first feature-length film in this style dissects a historical work of propaganda: In 2014, the “Islamic State” terror militia, then at the height of its territorial power, published an elaborately produced film entitled “Flames of War”, which many media outlets compared to the aesthetics of Hollywood blockbusters. Lee manages to abstract and defamiliarize the extreme violence of those images, but comes to the realisation that their ideological power cannot be decoded by the tools of film analysis alone. “Afterlives” broadens the perspective and looks for alternative models in dialogue with experts from the arts, political education and terrorism studies: They reconstruct destroyed cultural assets, develop strategies against extremist radicalisation and study what motivates people to leave terrorist groups. In all this, Lee’s intelligent essay never loses sight of the colonialist western image of the Middle East.

Boi tries to be quiet, but the glasses are shaking in his hand. You must not disturb Papa! Because when Papa is disturbed, the angry man in him wakes up and beats his beloved Mama. In “Angry Man”, there is no hiding from the violence that creeps into every fibre of daily life in the form of nervous anticipation or paralysing panic. Yet despite his fear, Boi does the only right thing: He goes to get help. But Killi’s film is not just the story of a brave boy who breaks the spiral of domestic violence: Her work radiates empathy in every direction, including even the father. Because he has a monster inside him – a drawn one that grows and creeps before it pushes its way out, where it erupts as a cut-out angry man. He needs help, too. “Angry Man”, the adaptation of a picture book by Gro Dahle and Svein Nyhus, conveys in a humanistic and credible manner that people can free themselves and change. All without a romanticising happy end.

films.t: Apocalypse Yesterday, Today, Tomorrow, and the Day After Tomorrow
films.ot: Apokalypsa včera, dnes, zítra a pozítří
films.syn: Can a state of emergency become normality? Is everyday life possible despite the apocalypse? Bohdan would reply with a “yes” and a calm smile. He lives in Nikopol, Ukraine, on the former Kakhovka Reservoir, which dried up rapidly after the Russian army destroyed the dam in 2023. Like most of Nikopol’s inhabitants, Bohdan has adapted to the constant bomb alarms and nearly daily bombardments – an unbelievable mental achievement which Anastasiia Bonadyha also captures using sound design and music, transforming it in the process: a music box plays a Viennese waltz, the howling sirens turn into the drawn-out tone of a shofar horn. Bohdan’s serenity and optimism are deeply rooted in his faith. As he puts it, he’s not scared of death, he will come to God anyway. Living and enduring, as long as possible: shot on a Super 8 camera, Bonadyha’s film is a moving time capsule, a moment of hope amid the impositions of the ongoing war.

Between 1959 and 1981, the Franco regime had over 33,000 bodies transferred from more than 500 mass graves across Spain to the Valle de los Caídos – a monumental mausoleum erected to glorify the fascist victory. Decades later, relatives are still searching for the remains of their loved ones. Three families follow in the footsteps of the disappeared and encounter bureaucratic, legal and social obstacles that persist to this day. Drawing on director Manuel Correa’s own research as part of Forensic Architecture, a research agency that investigates state and corporate violence, the film reconstructs in meticulous detail what the regime sought to conceal. Digital maps, citizens’ archives, official documents and new forensic technologies reveal what remained hidden for decades. The result is a topography of terror that visualises the extent of systematic violence and brings to light the history buried beneath fascist monumentalism.

Among hundreds of hours of unseen 1980s footage documenting the rehabilitation of Aubervilliers, a Parisian working-class suburb, filmmaker Giuseppe Schillaci recognised 15-year-old French-Algerian Fatsah Bouyahmed, then an ordinary boy who would later become an actor. Suffering memory loss after an accident, Fatsah agrees to revisit the neighbourhood he always wanted to leave through the archival footage. As the images are decoded, two recoveries of memory converge: Fatsah’s life and that of a 1980s working-class suburb. His stories of family and neighbours bring faces and lives out of the archival anonymity. A fluid dialogue between past and present, VHS footage and television archives, and fragments of Fatsah’s memory recreates the visual texture of the 80s while resurrecting forms of togetherness that, seen today, feel improbable.French and immigrant residents shared a belief in the common good through community work, neighbourhood TV, football, rap contests and collective efforts to improve life, as officials involved them in measures to tackle the “malaise of the suburbs.” A forgotten collective struggle, suspended between nostalgia, the elusive truth of memory and socio-politics, before the already lurking racism, segregation and economic inequalities hardened and later erupted in the rage of the banlieues. By connecting one man’s recovered memory to the unheard working-class voices Schillaci subtly plants a doubt: has our belief in the inevitability of today’s unjust realities made those forms of solidarity seem utopian, and is a better future still possible?

aw: Prize of the International Film Critics (FIPRESCI Prize)
ap.sel: Officially selected (section: International Competition Documentary Film)

films.syn: It speaks from the thick smoke, first with one voice, then with two. I already knew you, it says, when you still had no form, I see you. The voice is deep, it regrets its biggest mistake: creating civilisation, which has multiplied, spiralled out of control, become all-encompassing. Christopher Galinos’s atmospherically charged experimental film moves back and forth between a lament and a (bad) dream. We don’t know who we’re supposed to sympathise with here: is it the 3D creature akin to a wooden sculpture whose long hands hold a small ball? Or is it the male figures that come forth upon the shimmering fabric, eventually covering its entire surface? Are we these figures? Galinos confronts us with these questions and ideas about creation myths and releases us again, lost in thought.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: International Competition Animated Film)

films.syn: “You can’t seem to move forward, can you?” her mother asks. Twenty years after an unfinished film, the filmmaker is still pursuing her creative callings, confronting her roots, familial expectations and silences that have shaped her. An intimate essay about identity and belonging, set in a small rural Slovakian community where her creativity and sexuality clash with strict expectations of womanhood. Through personal archives, home movies and animation, she gently attempts to untangle what holds her back. Can she move forward without damaging the roots that are hers too?

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: International Competition Documentary Film)

films.ot: Em bé đồng bóng, em bé ngạo nghễ và em bé đau lòng
films.syn: When Quang’s sister Mai becomes pregnant out of the blue, one thing is clear to him: this new chapter in their lives will change the family forever. He picks up his camera. He works on the film on the film for seven years, collecting photos, diaries and telephone conversations. Using a DIY scrapbook aesthetic, he weaves the present together with memories and images from the past. We travel with Quang back to his youth in the northern Vietnamese province of Lào Cai near the Chinese border. Nine years his senior, his sister Mai introduces him to cool music and trendy fashion, while his mother Cuc dreams of a traditional family. This is a dream that is slipping ever further out of reach: her son is gay and her daughter is living with schizophrenia. As an adult, Quang moves to Hanoi, where he can finally feel free, and his distance from his family grows. Years later, Baby Guava brings Quang closer to his family again. The child brings them together, but also lays old tensions bare. Different ideas about what constitutes a “normal” life have long been met with silence. With brutal honesty and intimate, sometimes uncomfortable insights, Quang looks at his family and the unspoken pain and resentment that stand between them. And he also shows the hopes and efforts at finding understanding and acceptance despite everything in order to provide Baby Guava with a loving environment.

It looks like business as usual deep in the jungle – until one night a lantern lights up and magically attracts countless insects. They fall into a strange trance; even the bat family wake up. While the adults use the bright commotion to hunt, the young bat saves a glowworm, a fly and a moth. The next night, the dangerous light returns. The small bat is determined to try to save her new friends from its spell. A small adventure about friendship and mutual help.

A transmedia documentary based on three years of research on the Murg river, this work takes its shape in a manner inspired by the river itself. Images and sounds flow from one piece to another, forming a documentary that is alive rather than set in time and bound to a single frame. “Becoming River” has many parts, four of which are exhibited here. Two 2-channel video installations (FLUSSORAKEL and STAU/FALL) share the same surfaces and run in a continuous loop. FLUSSKINO is a selection of documentaries, fictions and performances filmed along the river. HYDROSPHÄRE is a sculpture of video monitors that give an insight into the flow of the Murg. SCHWEMMLAND is a sound installation based on live data sent from a probe on the Murg. By flowing through different media and projects, documenting the river for its nature, people and various identities, the piece becomes an investigation of a body over time, and the diversity by which one may be described.

A public swimming pool complex in the middle of a forest which is soon to be renovated: between water slides, French fries, TikTok and sun cream, six teenagers spend the long summer days in the “Badi”, as outdoor pools are called in Swiss German. It is a place to discuss, laugh, try things out and simply hang out together. Whether on the grass, in the water or between the different pools, their conversations revolve around everything that currently moves them. This sun-kissed film accompanies these adolescents at a moment of transition. They talk about the past, think about the future and try to find out who they are and how they will find their place in a changing world. The film stays close to their glances, conversations and encounters, taking an unvarnished look into the inner world of these adolescents – their curiosities, their humour, their contradictions and their insecurities. For one summer long, the Badi becomes a place where childhood and future can exist alongside each other. And while the orange slide is dismantled, the question of what will remain of this summer bubbles up through the water.

What is left when everything fades away? An old photographer tries to reconstruct people and events by means of old photographs, but they keep slipping away from him, vanishing in the dark, washed away by the waves. In his 2D animated film, rendered in black and white, Anton Dyakov not only shows how memories are lost, but also how they sometimes haunt and overwhelm us – for example in the shape of a disturbing archive fragment of blurred war photos. “Black Box” deals with loss and grief from a personal, yet universal perspective, while referencing the culture of remembrance in the digital age which is increasingly managing – or seeking to manage – without the haptic assurance of a printed photo.

Created using still and moving images sourced from NASA’s STEREO satellite solar observation mission, “Black Rain” turns unprocessed scientific data into a raw and glitched-out perspective on nearby interplanetary space. Embracing the artefacts, the film gives us an unmanicured and almost voyeuristic view of space, distant from the glamour of sci-fi or the carefully colourised images normally released by NASA to the press, as we track solar winds, coronal mass ejections and passing comets, sometimes recognisable only as blurs of lines and pixels, across a monochrome background of stars and the milky way.

The small kitchen table around which director Kamila Serwicka, her two sisters and their mother Agnieszka squeeze themselves has something symbolic about it: the space they each have while living together is restricted and somehow shrunk down; expansion is bitterly needed. Yet this crampedness also allows an intimacy to be experienced, a solidarity that supports and protects. In “Blossoming”, Serwicka creates a portrait of her family, who were profoundly affected by the alcoholism of the father and husband for many years. The tension when he enters the room is tangible – they all keep their distance in an attempt to shield themselves from verbal violence and emotional manipulation. Yet the film doesn’t remain in this oppressive status quo: when the addict leaves, a transition process begins which throws up sensitive questions. How was it possible to ensure such a situation for so long? Why did Agnieszka never separate from her husband? How will things now be? Over the course of five years, the Serwicka women expand their gaze, find new perspectives and standpoints – and new connections with each other, also in religious rituals. “Blossoming” bears witness to a both a challenging escape and a reawakening long overdue. A reminder that nothing has to stay the same.

aw: Prize of the Interreligious Jury
ap.sel: Officially selected (section: International Competition Documentary Film)

films.syn: April 2020: The playground is empty and quiet, with a sadly fluttering barrier tape that nobody cares about because everyone is at home in lockdown. Except for a pear-shaped 3D figure which pads searchingly through the gravelly sand on thin legs, in chunky sneakers. It is towing an exhausted balloon with a frozen smile and – chunky sneakers. The dangling balloon hands pat the lonely rule-breaker from above. Franz Impler’s poetic and playfully condensed snapshot lets us empathise with an indescribable, exceptional situation in all its melancholy and absurdity.

While taking care of her young daughter, the director makes jelly. She reflects on the birth of her child and her own excessive perfectionism, which also extends to her artistic practice. The simple dessert develops into a “zoetrope pudding”. Once she lets go of her need for precision and allows relaxed playfulness into the working process, she succeeds in making a multi-layered cinematic dish. Its ingredients: sugar, silicone, 3D-printing filament. Kateryna Voznytsia manages many things at once here: to intelligently bridge the gap between contemporary working methods and historical techniques from the early cinema era and sensitively question her role as a mother, woman and filmmaker, all while also maintaining a loving bond with her daughter.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: International Competition Animated Film)

films.syn: Bára Basiková is a Czech rock icon. She left a lasting impression in the 80s as lead singer of the bands Stromboli and Precedens and continues to fill concert halls as a solo artist to this day. Numerous musicals also live from her presence. Famous for her fascinating, approachable longitudinal portraits, Helena Třeštíková shows Basiková’s turbulent life over the decades. Her love of art and her search for fulfilling partnerships are recurring themes. More than once, Basiková is forced to admit that a relationship has failed and must risk a new start. Money repeatedly proves scarce and the burden of everyday life sometimes almost forces her to her knees. Yet Třeštíková never dwells too long in any one moment: the editing is fast-paced; over feature-film length, “Bára – Diary of a Rockstar” conveys a speed and richness of experience that seem to stand in direct relation to the protagonist’s lifestyle. Basiková is driven, a romantic and a fighter. Třeštíková brings substantial themes in her own unique way to the fore: what are the consequences of deciding to dedicate your existence to a passion full of uncertainties? What roles do age and aging play for a woman? And last, but not least, how to always keep things going?

aw: Prize of the Interreligious Jury Special Mention
ap.sel: Officially selected (section: International Competition Documentary Film)

films.syn: Camille, a very small girl, and the Chameleon who is afraid of heights are inseparable and love to play hide-and-seek in the forest. Camille loves to literally call the tune with her whistling. But one day she becomes too cocky and gives Chameleon an idea that will upset everything. Now they are lost in the green thicket. Can they get over their pride and find each other again?

Ugo Ulive left his native Uruguay in 1967 to move to the Venezuelan capital of Caracas, where two years later he realised three short films at the newly founded Centro de Cine Documental de la Universidad de los Andes: “Caracas: dos o tres cosas”, “Diamantes” and “Basta!”. The latter was part of the Leipzig retrospective “Film in the People’s Struggle for Liberation: Latin America” in 1972. Inspired by Antonin Artaud’s concept of the “Theatre of Cruelty”, it stands out for disturbing images of an autopsy that reveal the degree of dehumanisation under the influence of imperialism. In “Caracas: dos o tres cosas”, also in the form of an experimental collage, Ulive, roaming the streets of Caracas with his camera, contrasts the public face of a divided society with audio fragments from radio, advertising and pop music.

Sam, a grumpy raccoon, must share a prison cell with Bob, a loveable, but somewhat slow-witted manatee. Their chaotic prison break gradually reveals Sam’s soft core, while Bob remains unfailingly loyal to Sam. Will they manage to escape? Suddenly, that no longer matters so much, since together they have already experienced something much better: solidarity. A cute plasticine animation you will absolutely love.

A tennis player is driven to despair by his opponent, a devious blue Cheshire cat. After her serve, she uses wicked magic to manipulate the spatial coordinates and establishes the one, ruthless rule: Now the court keeps rotating and with every return the player, long-since destined to lose, crowns himself the invincible opponent. A creative tennis nightmare.

Anne (36) lives in Halle (Saale) and her life is in chaos. An apartment full of moving boxes, a yapping dog. She tells her mother on the phone that the electricity is about to be cut off again. Sometimes her daughter Leonie (14) drops by. Like her mother, she is at risk of slipping into drug addiction. Anne has already lost custody of her two younger children, too. The camera stays purely observational, captures loose scenes from the life of a woman who wants to take responsibility again. The film does not look for psychological explanations but shows Anne as she is. On her drives through the prefabricated housing estate, she seems isolated from her surroundings. Mother and daughter grow closer over an ice cream in a public square. Anne’s visit to her mother provides support but creates pressure, too. We grow ever closer to Anne, sharing her wish that she can become a role model for her daughter.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: German Competition Documentary Film)

films.syn: The Europe-wide protests against Chile’s military dictatorship were expressed not only by political activism, but by a host of artistic actions. The colourful aesthetics of the Unidad Popular’s street art, popularised by the Ramona Parra Brigades, became a visual trademark. Based on this model, the Brigada Pablo Neruda, for example, whose members included well-known Chilean artists exiled in Paris like José Balmes, Gracia Barrios and Guillermo Núñez, realised a 60-metre-long mural on the fringes of documenta 6 in Kassel in 1977. Its creation was documented in Franz Lehmkuhl’s film “Chilenische Wandmalerei” (1977–80), screened in Leipzig in 1980. In his agitation film “Chile lebt”, co-produced with Michael Börner, the Chilean journalist and filmmaker Juan Forch uses pictures of the Brigada Pablo Neruda to express what keeps hope in his homeland alive: international solidarity. In 1979, Forch returned to Chile from exile in the GDR.

Pesticides wipe out the insects, the oil spills into the ocean, the forests burn: In 1994, director Laila Rakvåg let a bird fly over and through the ecological, human-made hotspots that plague us even today to a far worse extent. Sometimes the bird is able to land in beautiful natural surroundings, but the rest is never permanent, paradise is always on the brink of the next hellish transformation. The further the bird flies, the more human its features become: It becomes a baby that is then actually born – and carries the memories of the bird in its newly opened eyes. We are inseparably linked to nature; what we do to it, we do to ourselves: Rakvåg’s film is an activist plea for more empathy with our planet and a change of thinking, told from the perspective of an expectant mother.

16-year-old Krzysztof was last seen on a bridge over Poland’s Vistula River in 2023. The CCTV camera briefly turned away, and by the time it returned, he had vanished. Following his disappearance, his father Daniel launches a relentless search in Poland’s largest river. As time piles up, the searches persist. Any tech that proves useful gets pulled into it, from drones to metal detectors, trackers, and even loaves of bread, sent floating down the current in the hope of locating the body. The camera matches these rhythms, dredging the river’s depths and combing its banks. The searches, showing the father’s restless energy and the sheer labour of this endeavour, mix with vérité scenes with his family, as well as news snippets about Krzysztof’s alleged sightings. Social media streams are scoured too, providing unsettling insights into the boy’s inner states. Director Michał Marczak – and by extension his camera – accompany Daniel, taking the audience along in a boat and into the heart of a family’s unresolved grief. As closure remains out of reach, Daniel starts assisting other searches, and sombre discoveries are made of other lives lost in the waters.

A tiny fish swims through a huge underwater world. It is loud and hectic at times. He would love nothing better than to hide behind the other fish. Is he too small to see the world as the big ones see it? Drawn in enchanting blue and green watercolours, this animation shows that there is no such thing as too big or too small. And wouldn’t it be lovely if we could all fly up to heaven in a big bubble in the end?

films.t: Cold River: I Am in Leipzig
films.ot: Lěng Shuǐ Jiāng: Wǒ Zài Lái Bǐ Xī
films.syn: Haiguang dreams. Of his dead grandmother, his birthplace Lěng Shuǐ Jiāng in China, his performances and art projects and his job at a wholesale warehouse in Leipzig. But Haiguang not only dreams, he also films. Himself and his surroundings. Persistent, stoical, sometimes with a handheld camera, sometimes using a tripod – knowing that there is another layer under one’s everyday life that can only be perceived if one dares to search for meaning beyond the visible. If you dare to lie down on a crossing in the park and wait for what happens.
